catalog_locator: Ch. 6 'Word stress', pp. 64-66 (6.1 Stress of roots) and p. 70 (6.3); summary in Ch. 1, pp. 3-4
catalog_quote: [p.64] In roots of more than one syllable, word stress is generally on the second syllable. But a small group of disyllabic verbs have initial stress, and polysyllabic roots of other word classes are sometimes stressed on the first, the third or (very rarely) the fourth syllable. Suffixes fall into two main groups: stress-attracting suffixes, which are always stressed, and stress-neutral suffixes, which are never stressed. Unintegrated Russian loan words keep their Russian stress. ... [p.65] Most native non-verbal roots are monosyllabic. The overwhelming majority of polysyllabic non-verbal roots, whether native roots or Oriental loans, are stressed on the second syllable. ... This tendency for stress on the second syllable is so strong that even Russian loanwords are sometimes stressed on the second syllable. ... audit.recode_to: classification fixed-strict (second stress, counts as exceptionless (the strict set), domain word) -> morphological / root-lexical accent in a left two-syllable window: stress on the 2nd syllable of polysyllabic roots (dominant, with listed lexical exceptions), monosyllabic root + stress-neutral suffixes = INITIAL stress, stress-attracting suffixes always stressed; i.e. peninitial is 'dominant for roots', not 'strict for words'. If the scheme must keep a positional label: peninitial, not in the strict set, domain ROOT/STEM rather than word. This matches the record's own qv 'set by morphology' and WALS 15A 'Left-edge: first or second'.

sources.quote: Lezgian has pronounced stress inside the initial two-syllable window, but this regularity does not hold for numerous loans. In native words, stress is normally located on the post-initial syllable if the initial one is open. sources.quote: Instrumental (one Yargun-dialect speaker), on pretonic high-vowel syncope; stress placement is taken from Haspelmath 1993 ('The very detailed description of the facts given in Haspelmath's grammar ... served as starting point'). Examples mark second-syllable root stress (thwk'úl 'knife') and stress shift to the stress-attracting plural/oblique suffixes (thwk'ul-ár, rath-íni); Table 1: root vowel 128.1 ms when stressed (abs. sg.) vs 70.15 / 64.6 ms when stress shifts to the suffix (abs. pl., erg. sg.): 'stress shift away from the vowel affects vowel duration to a large extent'.
